findings: Use customs for the trade baseline
SARS records 10.793 bn litres of diesel imports and 0.796 of exports in 2024: net imports of 9.997 bn litres.
Reconcile the sales proxy
FIASA reports 20.763 bn litres of petrol/diesel sales. Editions conflict; this is an unverified consumption proxy.
Do not call the residual production
Sales less net imports leaves 7.685 bn litres. Production, stock changes and coverage must explain that residual.
4.action: Manish: match production, trade and stocks by product/year. Nigel: agree the sales source before forecasting.

findings: Concentrate the first customer tests
Gauteng, KZN and Western Cape hold 68.6% of reported 2022 sales. Vopak sites sit in the top two provinces.
Use consistent reporting regions
Eastern: EC/KZN. Inland: GP/FS/LP/MP/NW. Western: WC. Other: NC. These groups align the demand and storage tests.
Establish access customer by customer
Provincial sales locate the market; they do not prove terminal reach, customer rights or Vopak deliveries.
5.action: Nigel: select Durban/Lesedi customer destinations. Manish: retain observed 2022 sales and label later estimates.

findings: Start with the observed pattern
Gauteng remains the largest province through 2013–2022. Volumes were broadly steady, with a clear pandemic dip.
Keep 2024 estimates separate
Petrol estimates hold 2022 shares: GP 3.47, KZN 1.47 and WC 1.41 bn litres. These are not observed provincial sales.
Resolve the remaining source choices
Manish fixed the 2013 parser and traced 2015 to a revision. The 2014 conflict and incomplete 2018 coverage still need decisions.
6.action: Manish: close the source choices. Nigel: decide whether held-share petrol estimates support the outlook; test diesel separately.

findings: Use sourced provincial totals
The total bars use reported 2022 petrol/diesel sales. This establishes provincial demand, not where the fuel came from.
Treat origin shares as an example
Domestic/import segments are authored illustrations. No measured provincial supply-origin allocation is established.
Close the national balance first
Match production, exports and stock movements to the demand year before allocating an import requirement to provinces.
7.action: Manish: reconcile the national balance, then obtain origin/destination evidence. Keep unsupported provincial origin unknown.

findings: Plan around the smaller footprint
Published capacity falls from 718 to 358 thousand bbl/day between 2020 and 2022. A restart remains conditional.
Use output for the fuel balance
FY2024 output is 29.1 million barrels at Secunda and 17.8 for Sasol’s Natref share; both cover all products and fiscal years.
Keep the restart as a separate case
Match yields, downtime and calendar years before estimating imports. Nameplate capacity does not establish petrol/diesel output.
9.action: Manish: build the product/year output bridge. Henry: review plant assumptions. Nigel: agree conditional restart timing.

findings: Use road cost as the first screen
Darker cells show lower illustrative road cost from Durban or Lesedi. Fuel price, storage and pipeline tariffs are excluded.
Keep grey areas unassessed
Grey marks no assessed connection under the schematic rule. It does not establish that a customer is unreachable.
Prove the full service proposition
Pipeline/rail lines are context. Route capacity, product compatibility, receipt/dispatch and customer rights still need evidence.
11.action: Nigel: choose a destination and cost/service threshold. Manish: replace example rates with dated route quotes and access evidence.

findings: Keep Durban in the inland comparison
Durban and Lesedi form Vopak’s SA footprint. Compare their full delivered service with alternatives for the same customer.
Test the eastern alternative
Matola’s GIMTL lists 60,000 m³ of petrol/diesel tanks. Test availability, N4 route cost and customer access.
Test the western alternative
Walvis Bay’s NOSF lists 65,000 m³ of petrol/diesel capacity. Test the Trans-Kalahari route on the same cost/service basis.
12.action: Manish: compare one product and destination across all three gateways. Nigel: agree the service standard and commercial access test.

findings: Anchor the test in Durban and Lesedi
Vopak lists 360,200 m³ in Durban and 140,000 m³ at Lesedi. These anchor the eastern and inland customer tests.
Verify working fuel capacity
Published gross tankage covers mixed products. It does not establish usable petrol/diesel space, annual deliveries or customer share.
Keep coverage gaps explicit
Missing operator capacities remain unknown. Conditional Transnet leases are excluded from the operating bars.
13.action: Manish: confirm fuel-compatible working space and dispatch by site. Nigel: obtain operating data for Durban and Lesedi.

findings: Remove inter-terminal transfers
The example includes 1.8 bn litres transferred through both Durban and Lesedi. Counting both receipts would count that fuel twice.
Use 3.0 in this illustration
Receipts of 2.8 plus 2.0, less the shared 1.8 transfer, leave 3.0 bn litres of unique deliveries. Actual throughput is unverified.
Establish served demand before growth
Match customer, product and period records. The opportunity waterfall on page 15 then removes already-served volumes once.
14.action: Nigel: obtain customer deliveries and transfer records. Manish: reconcile unique served volumes before estimating growth.

findings: Test turnover against operating data
Two monthly turns is an authored base, not a verified SA site rate. The appendix tests one and three turns.
Estimate achievable handling
Use compatible working space, downtime and receipt/dispatch limits. Gross tankage alone overstates what may be handled.
Avoid a regional shortage conclusion
Inland inventory omits material operators. Coastal tanks can serve inland demand, and transfers can count the same fuel twice.
16.action: Manish: verify working capacity and unique dispatch. Nigel: obtain site records. Replace common turns with site-specific evidence.
